method_notes: Cross-city survey of dedicated, nonprofit/community-controlled folk & traditional music/dance facilities across the 20 largest US metros (Census MSA definitions). Research was split across 5 background research agents (4 metros each), each using web_search sparingly for discovery and web_fetch of org sites/Wikipedia/news for verification; every entry below is sourced to a specific URL gathered that way. FINDING: density of owned/controlled real estate correlates strongly with density of recurring folk activity. Metros with a historic immigrant-ethnic-hall tradition plus active folk nonprofits that bought or secured long-term buildings -- Minneapolis-St Paul (6 controlled facilities: Tapestry Folkdance Center 1999, Cedar Cultural Center 1989, Celtic Junction 2009/2016, American Swedish Institute 1929, Norway House 2015, Danish American Center), Chicago (6: Old Town School's two owned campuses plus four ethnic halls), San Francisco/Berkeley (5: Freight & Salvage 2009, Ashkenaz 1997, Swedish American Hall 1907, Finnish Hall 1932, Croatian Cultural Center), Seattle (4: Swedish Cultural Center, Leif Erikson Hall, National Nordic Museum, Phinney Neighborhood Center -- leased 1981, purchased 2009), Denver (4: Swallow Hill 1999, Wheat Ridge Grange, Denver Turnverein, Trollheim Lodge), and Houston (4, mostly Czech/German fraternal halls) -- show the heaviest, most frequent recurring programming (Swallow Hill ~20 events/month, Old Town School dozens/month, Freight & Salvage ~25/month, Tapestry ~9/month, Ashkenaz ~18/month). By contrast, Sun Belt / newer-growth metros with weak ethnic-hall inheritance and little folk-nonprofit real estate activity -- Atlanta, Miami, Tampa, and Riverside -- show ZERO qualifying controlled facilities; Dallas-Fort Worth, Orlando, and Phoenix show exactly one each (and Phoenix's is a public facility run by a nonprofit partner, not nonprofit-owned). Washington DC also shows only one clean example (Glen Echo Park's Spanish Ballroom) despite being an old, large metro -- its folk infrastructure (Institute of Musical Traditions, Greater Washington Ceili Club, FSGW) is almost entirely built on rented church/community space. The LOSSES list reinforces the mechanism: every confirmed loss involved an organization that did not own its building -- Detroit's Lovett Hall contra series (evicted with 4 days' notice, Dec 2004, after 23.5 years), DC's Potter's House (2026, lost access when it could not secure the building after a funding/sponsorship change), NYC's Peoples' Voice Cafe (its host church sold the building for ~$66M in 2023-24), NYC's Gerde's Folk City (1986, rent nearly tripled with an unaffordable conditional lease), and a wave of 1960s-70s folk coffeehouses nationwide (Ash Grove LA, Boarding House SF, Sand Mountain Houston, Heritage Coffee House San Diego, The Flick Miami, Scottsdale's folk-coffeehouse row) that burned, lost leases, or simply could not survive without a stable, owned home. The clearest counter-example to 'ownership guarantees survival' is the Swedish Club of Chicago, which owned its clubhouse from 1896 but still closed in 1984 due to membership decline -- ownership helps resilience against landlords, not against demographic change. Caveats: several entries are 'weak fits' (museums or general-purpose ethnic halls where folk dance/music is now only an occasional rather than core/recurring activity -- flagged in notes); a few ownership details (e.g., Trollheim Lodge Denver, Finnish Hall Berkeley, Jalopy Theatre NYC) could not be fully confirmed from primary sources and are flagged accordingly; 'events_per_month' is left null wherever no publisher-stated figure was found (most venues do not publish an aggregate monthly count, so null is the norm, not an omission). Metros with no documented facility-loss case in available sources (Philadelphia, Minneapolis, Tampa, Seattle, Riverside, Dallas-Fort Worth, Orlando) are treated as genuine research gaps, not confirmed absence of losses.

facilities.name: Irish Arts Center
facilities.notes: Original building at 553 W. 51st St.; completed a $60M new adjoining building at 726 11th Ave c.2022. Traditional Irish music/dance (seisiuns, ceili, step dance classes) core to programming.

facilities.name: Jalopy Theatre and School of Music
facilities.org: Living Traditions (nonprofit partner) / founders Geoff & Lynette Wiley
facilities.notes: Building purchased personally by the Wiley family in 2006; unclear whether the nonprofit partner Living Traditions holds title. Ambiguous ownership, coded precarious pending verification.

facilities.name: Ukrainian National Home
facilities.org: Ukrainian National Home of NYC, Inc.
facilities.notes: Community hub since the late 1960s, historically hosting Ukrainian folk music/dance; also operates an on-site restaurant.

facilities.name: Germania Park (Deutscher Schul- und Gesang Verein)
facilities.org: Deutscher Schul- und Gesang Verein, Inc.
facilities.notes: Club founded 1895; land purchased 1925; ballroom added 1935, expanded 1966. Annual Oktoberfest, German choral/folk dance events.

facilities.name: Irish Cultural Centre of Greater Boston
facilities.org: Irish Cultural Centre of Greater Boston
facilities.notes: 61-acre campus with performance/function space; partners with Comhaltas Ceoltoiri Eireann Boston branch for ceili dances.

facilities.name: South Boston Lithuanian Citizens' Association
facilities.notes: Member-owned since founding; banquet hall/bar plus Lithuanian cultural events.

facilities.name: Scandinavian Cultural Center & Library (Nordic Hall)
facilities.org: Scandinavian Charitable Society of Greater Boston
facilities.notes: Nordic Hall opened 2001; Sons of Norway's Norumbega Lodge uses hall for folk dance/meetings as a guest, not owner; merged with Scandinavian Library 2024.

facilities.name: Club Passim
facilities.notes: Continuous presence at 47 Palmer St. since 1963 (60+ years) but as a renter, not owner; successor to Club 47 (1958) and for-profit Passim (1969-94). 'Over 400 performances per year' per own materials.

facilities.name: Commodore John Barry Arts and Cultural Center (The Irish Center)
facilities.notes: Corporation formed Jan 1958 specifically to buy the building. Weekly set-dance lessons + ceili dances 2nd/4th Fridays + monthly Ceili Og. Philadelphia Ceili Group is resident but does not itself own the building.

facilities.name: Cannstatter Volksfest-Verein
facilities.notes: German-American hall; signature annual Labor Day weekend Volksfest with German folk dance/music.

facilities.name: Danube Swabian Association of Philadelphia and Vicinity
facilities.org: Danube Swabian Association of Philadelphia and Vicinity
facilities.notes: Annual Trachtenfest and Tag der Donauschwaben feature traditional Donauschwaben folk dance.

facilities.name: Spanish Ballroom, Glen Echo Park
facilities.org: National Park Service + Glen Echo Park Partnership for Arts & Culture, Inc.
facilities.notes: NPS owns/manages grounds; nonprofit partnership (created 2002 by Montgomery County) runs the arts/dance programming. Regular contra, swing, international folk, tango, waltz nights.

facilities.name: Old Town School of Folk Music — Lincoln Square campus
facilities.org: Old Town School of Folk Music
facilities.notes: Renovated 1929 Hild Library building. Daily classes plus dozens of concerts/month.

facilities.name: Old Town School of Folk Music — Lincoln Park campus (Armitage/Aldine Hall)
facilities.org: Old Town School of Folk Music
facilities.notes: Board voted unanimously Oct 2018 to sell this owned building; reversed decision March 2019 after community/student backlash -- shows ownership alone doesn't fully insulate a flagship space from the market.

facilities.name: Irish American Heritage Center
facilities.notes: Purchased former 1927 Mayfair School building 1985, opened 1986. Weekly Tue set-dance lessons, 1st/3rd Fri ceili, 1st Sat Celtic Social Dance.

facilities.name: Croatian Cultural Center of Chicago
facilities.notes: Home of the Hrvatska Loza folklore/tamburitza ensemble; dance floor/banquet hall.

facilities.name: Lithuanian World Center
facilities.notes: Supports 50+ constituent organizations including folk-dance ensembles.

facilities.name: Swedish American Museum
facilities.notes: Weak fit: folk dance only at seasonal events (Midsommarfest, St. Lucia), not a weekly program.

facilities.name: Tapestry Folkdance Center
facilities.notes: Bought its building Oct 16 1999 after a 1998 rent-tripling threat at its previous rented space (Sabathani Community Center). Weekly Sat contra + weekly Fri international folk dance.

facilities.name: Celtic Junction Arts Center
facilities.notes: Building bought 2009 by founders Cormac O'Se & Natalie O'Shea; CJAC nonprofit formalized 2016 and controls programming (building itself not deeded to CJAC -- long-term control, not outright nonprofit ownership). Weekly square dance + regular concerts/classes.

facilities.name: The Cedar Cultural Center
facilities.org: Minnesota STAR (Society for Traditional Arts and Resources)
facilities.notes: Built 1948 as a movie theater; donated to the nonprofit in 1989. Multiple weekly concerts; home of the Global Roots Festival.

facilities.name: American Swedish Institute
facilities.notes: 1908 mansion donated 1929; Nelson Cultural Center addition 2012. Seasonal/periodic Nordic dance (Midsommar) rather than weekly.

facilities.name: Norway House
facilities.notes: Org founded 2004; building opened 2015, major expansion 2022. Periodic cultural events/exhibits.

facilities.name: Danish American Center
facilities.notes: Folk dancing cited as part of regular programming; founding/acquisition year not independently confirmed (gap).

facilities.name: Finnish Center Association
facilities.notes: ~60-year-old Scandinavian/Nordic hall. Hosts 'Nordic Heritage Folk Dance' practices; frequency not published.

facilities.name: Ukrainian Cultural Center of Metropolitan Detroit
facilities.notes: Org incorporated 1956; building purchased/opened 1978. Primarily banquet/rental use; recurring folk-dance programming not confirmed.

facilities.name: Freight & Salvage Coffeehouse
facilities.org: Berkeley Society for the Preservation of Traditional Music
facilities.notes: Incorporated as nonprofit 1983; purpose-built 490-seat LEED building at 2020 Addison St. opened Aug 27 2009 after a ~$12M decade-long capital campaign with City of Berkeley support.

facilities.name: Ashkenaz Music & Dance Community Center
facilities.notes: Purchased by a cooperative of patrons/staff/musicians after founder David Nadel's 1996 murder; reopened under nonprofit ownership June 1997. Weekly klezmer/Balkan/Cajun-zydeco/contra/international folk dance nights.

facilities.name: Swedish American Hall
facilities.notes: Built 1907 after the 1906 earthquake destroyed the prior Scandia Hall. Nonprofit still owns the building but leased/sold commercial operations (Cafe Du Nord) to private operators in 2013-14, diminishing community folk use -- a 'soft loss' short of closure.

facilities.name: Finnish Hall (Berkeley)
facilities.notes: Built 1932 by volunteers from local Finnish immigrant families. Hosts rentals, classes, and dances; precise legal ownership entity not fully confirmed (gap).

facilities.name: Croatian American Cultural Center of San Francisco
facilities.org: Croatian Cultural Center of San Francisco
facilities.notes: Tamburitza music and Croatian folk dance/festivals; founding/acquisition year not found in available sources (gap).

facilities.name: Swedish Cultural Center (formerly The Swedish Club)
facilities.notes: Current mid-century-modern building constructed 1959-61, funded entirely by the club through member bonds/donations; now a Seattle Landmark. Membership peaked ~5,000 in the 1970s, now ~1,100.

facilities.name: Leif Erikson Hall (Sons of Norway)
facilities.org: Sons of Norway, Leif Erikson Lodge 2-001
facilities.notes: Lodge organized 1903; current hall built 1986 largely by volunteer labor. Home of the 'Leikarringen' Norwegian folk dance group.

facilities.name: National Nordic Museum
facilities.notes: Founded 1980 in a former school building; moved to new purpose-built home 2018, renamed 2019. Primarily a museum -- weaker fit than Leif Erikson Hall for 'regular folk programming,' periodic folk dance festivals in partnership with the Lodge.

facilities.name: Phinney Neighborhood Center
facilities.org: Phinney Neighborhood Association (building) / Seattle Folklore Society (programming)
facilities.notes: Former John B. Allen Elementary School (built 1904); PNA leased it from Seattle School District starting 1981, purchased the campus 2009 after a capital campaign. Seattle Folklore Society's 'Emerald City Contra Dance' runs almost every Friday.

facilities.name: Japanese American Cultural & Community Center (JACCC)
facilities.notes: Campus built 1980-83 including Noguchi-designed plaza and Japanese Garden. Bon Odori (traditional Japanese folk dance) is centerpiece of the annual Nisei Week festival -- annual rather than monthly cadence.

facilities.name: Plaza de la Raza
facilities.place: Lincoln Park/Lincoln Heights, Los Angeles, CA
facilities.notes: City of Los Angeles owns the land/historic buildings in Lincoln Park; Plaza de la Raza operates under a long-term ground lease as primary tenant/programmer of Mexican/Chicano folklorico dance and arts education.

facilities.name: Ararat-Eskijian Museum and Research Center
facilities.notes: First Armenian museum on the West Coast, sited on the nonprofit Ararat Home campus. Weak fit: primarily a museum/research center, regular folk dance/music programming not confirmed.

facilities.name: Houston Saengerbund / Saengerhalle
facilities.notes: German choral/cultural society founded 1883. Owned Feagan St. property ~70 years until sold 2004; rented a church 2004-2022; purchased the former Heights Christian Church in 2022 (now 'Saengerhalle'). Folk dance mainly at Oktoberfest/Christmas concert.

facilities.name: SPJST Lodge 88
facilities.org: SPJST (Slavonic Benevolent Order of the State of Texas), Lodge 88
facilities.notes: Czech fraternal lodge hall; current (3rd) building dedicated 1965. Weekly bingo (not folk); Czechfest annual plus occasional polka dances -- genuinely 'folk' programming is episodic, not the hall's main year-round purpose.

facilities.name: Sokol Houston (T.J. Sokol of Houston)
facilities.notes: Czech gymnastic/cultural hall chartered 1951 (part of the Sokol movement founded 1862). Primary mission is gymnastics; folk dance is secondary, not confirmed as regularly scheduled.

facilities.name: Czech Center Museum Houston
facilities.notes: Purpose-built facility, construction began 2002, opened 2004. Weak fit: functions mainly as a museum; folk dance/kroje appear at festivals, not as a standing recurring series.

facilities.name: SPJST Lodge #92 'National Hall'
facilities.notes: Historic Czech-heritage dance hall, present building built 1938. ~Monthly 'Country and Western Dance' (1st Sunday) plus annual Cowtown Birthplace of Western Swing Festival -- recurring programming is adjacent to, rather than squarely, 'folk/traditional'.

facilities.name: German American Society of Central Florida
facilities.org: German American Society of Central Florida, Inc.
facilities.notes: Nonprofit social club founded 1963; purchased the Casselberry clubhouse 1972. Home of the Alpenrose Schuhplattler dance group; two Oktoberfests, Springtoberfest, Nacht in Wien, Narrensitzung, Heimatabend annually. Strongest clear-cut match found across the four Sun Belt metros researched in this group.

facilities.name: Swallow Hill Music (Daniels Hall / Tuft Theatre)
facilities.notes: Grew out of Harry Tuft's 1962 Denver Folklore Center. Purchased a former church building via ~$800K capital campaign for its 20th anniversary (1999). ~250 concerts/year across Daniels Hall (~300 seats) and Tuft Theatre (140 seats), plus a large year-round music school.

facilities.name: Wheat Ridge Grange No. 155
facilities.notes: Grange-owned hall hosting 2nd/4th Friday contra dances via CFOOTMAD programming. Borderline fit -- general community hall, only partly 'mainly folk' in programming.

facilities.name: Denver Turnverein (German House)
facilities.notes: Colorado's oldest organization of its type; current building built 1921. Weak fit: current primary programming is general ballroom/social/swing/tango dance; German folk dance (Schuhplattler) occurs mainly at Oktoberfest, not as a regular monthly folk series.

facilities.name: Trollheim Lodge (Sons of Norway 6-110)
facilities.org: Sons of Norway Trollheim Lodge / Trollheim Building Corporation
facilities.notes: Ownership inferred via an affiliated 'Trollheim Building Corporation' filed 1990 (common Sons of Norway practice); not independently confirmed via primary source (lodge's own site returned HTTP 403). Flagged as a gap needing deed/assessor verification.

facilities.name: Irish Cultural Center and McClelland Library
facilities.org: Irish Cultural & Learning Foundation (ICLF) + City of Phoenix Parks and Recreation
facilities.notes: City of Phoenix owns land/buildings; ICLF operates it under a public/private partnership. Monthly 'Third Friday' Ceili dance in the Great Hall plus weekly Tuesday Phoenix International Folk Dancers sessions.

facilities.name: House of Pacific Relations International Cottages
facilities.org: House of Pacific Relations (HPR) + City of San Diego Park & Recreation Dept.
facilities.notes: Cottages built for the 1935 California Pacific International Exposition; City owns land/cottages, ~30-38 member-nation nonprofit 'house' associations hold long-term stewardship/operational rights. Weekend 'Lawn Programs' with folk dance/music/food held nearly every weekend; includes House of Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Scotland, Ireland.

facilities.name: German American Societies of San Diego
facilities.org: German American Societies of San Diego, Inc.
facilities.notes: Incorporated 1965 as successor to the historic San Diego Turners after a 1945 fire destroyed Concordia Hall and the Turners disbanded in the 1980s. Biergarten; German folk dance groups (KinderTanzGruppe, BoogieTanz); annual Maifest, Oktoberfest, Weihnachtsmarkt.

facilities.name: San Diego International Folk Dance Club at Balboa Park Club
facilities.org: San Diego International Folk Dance Club
facilities.notes: Long-running weekly Wednesday user of a City of San Diego-owned ballroom, but no long-term lease document found specific to this club -- weaker fit than HPR, coded precarious/public-use rather than confirmed long-term control.

losses.name: Gerde's Folk City
losses.reason: Building owners nearly tripled rent and offered only a conditional 15-year lease requiring costly soundproofing the club couldn't afford; it never owned its space at any of its locations (11 W. 4th St. 1960-70; 130 W. 3rd St. 1970-86).

losses.name: Peoples' Voice Cafe (at Community Church of New York)
losses.reason: Hosted for years in a rented church (Community Church of New York) it did not own; the church sold the property to developer Continuum Company for ~$66.2M in 2023-24 for demolition/luxury condo tower, forcing relocation in 2024 to another borrowed space (Judson Memorial Church).

losses.name: Club 47 (original, 47 Mount Auburn St.)
losses.reason: Closed 1968 as the first folk boom waned; the brand was later revived as Passim (1969) at a new rented address, not a true reopening in the same owned building.

losses.name: The Potter's House
losses.reason: Coffeehouse/bookstore/folk open-mic venue run by Church of the Saviour community for 65+ years without ever owning the building; closed Jan 2026 after separating from its prior fiscal sponsor left it without funds and 'no access to the building,' per its own announcement.

losses.name: Swedish Club of Chicago
losses.reason: Closed due to membership decline/assimilation, NOT a landlord/tenure failure -- the club owned its clubhouse continuously from 1896 to 1984. Included as a counter-example showing ownership protects against landlords but not against demographic decline.

losses.name: Lovett Hall contra dance series (Henry Ford Museum/Greenfield Village)
losses.reason: Henry Ford Museum/Greenfield Village gave organizers only 4 days' notice in December 2004 that Lovett Hall -- a ballroom Henry Ford built to support his own passion for contra/square dancing -- would no longer be available; the 23.5-year-old monthly series (then 'the longest-running dance series in Michigan') ended with a final closing celebration Feb 6 2005. The Detroit/Ann Arbor contra scene never regained an equivalent dedicated hall, relying since on rotating rented churches/community halls (AACTMAD, Detroit Folk School).

losses.name: Ash Grove
losses.reason: Legendary folk/blues/bluegrass club destroyed by the third of a series of arson fires on Nov 11 1973; founder Ed Pearl never owned a fireproof/dedicated building, so a single structural loss ended the club outright.

losses.name: Golden Bear
losses.reason: Huntington Beach folk/rock club closed 1986 due to required seismic retrofit costs, redevelopment pressure, and sale of the property; the building was demolished later that year.

losses.name: The Boarding House
losses.reason: Music/comedy club destroyed by fire in 1980; reopened at a new North Beach location in 1982 but closed permanently in 1984 after founder David Allen's death -- never achieved stable owned premises.

losses.name: San Pablo Avenue folk-club corridor (Blind Lemon, Cabale Creamery, Jabberwock, Questing Beast)
losses.reason: A cluster of Berkeley folk clubs mostly closed by the early 1970s as the commercial folk wave faded and rents/tastes shifted; Freight & Salvage is the sole survivor of this scene specifically because it transitioned to nonprofit status and eventually bought its own building.

losses.name: Sand Mountain Coffee House
losses.reason: Iconic alcohol-free folk coffeehouse (incubator for Guy Clark, Townes Van Zandt, Jerry Jeff Walker) closed amid declining audiences, a failed pivot to serving alcohol, and the founder's declining health -- it never had a permanent institutional/nonprofit ownership structure.

losses.name: Houston Saengerbund's Feagan Street hall
losses.reason: Owned and occupied for roughly 70 years, sold in 2004 due to rising costs; the organization then rented space at a church for 18 years before purchasing its current Saengerhalle building in 2022.

losses.name: Red Light Cafe
losses.reason: Long-running folk/acoustic/Americana listening room forced to leave its Amsterdam Walk location due to wholesale redevelopment of the retail district into new commercial/residential space; relocating into the former Star Community Bar space in 2027.

losses.name: Denver Folklore Center Concert Hall
losses.reason: Harry Tuft's concert-hall operation lost roughly $15,000/year as the surrounding neighborhood declined in the late 1970s and the folk boom waned, facing loss of its lease; supporters spun off the nonprofit Swallow Hill Music Association (1979) to carry on the mission, eventually buying its own building in 1999.

losses.name: The Heritage Coffee House
losses.reason: Pioneering Mission Beach folk coffeehouse (launched Tom Waits' career) closed in 1973 amid the general early-1970s coffeehouse-closure wave tied to changing musical tastes and lease/economic pressures; the building is now a surf bar.

losses.name: The Flick
losses.reason: University of Miami-area folk coffeehouse (hosted Joni Mitchell, Jimmy Buffett, Jerry Jeff Walker early in their careers) closed in 1974 as the national folk-coffeehouse circuit contracted; site is now a restaurant.

losses.name: The Mews / Lumber Mill / Foggy Mountain Coffee House
losses.reason: Trio of Scottsdale folk coffeehouses where John Denver and Dolan Ellis performed early in their careers; all closed decades ago as ownership changed hands and the folk-coffeehouse wave ended -- precise closure dates/reasons not well documented in available sources.
